newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia mercy death man joked until the end.
newsitem.headline: Australia mercy death man joked until the end.

text.p: Bob Dent, the Australian who became the first man in the world to commit legally assisted suicide, was a kind, humorous man who found solace in Buddhism and helping fellow cancer sufferers.
At his funeral in a tin-shed Buddhist temple on Friday, friends and family paid tribute to the former Church of England missionary who was struck by prostate cancer five years ago.

One friend told the funeral service he was a "gentleman, a craftsman and a very generous individual...his acceptance and lack of fear of the inevitable should be a good example and inspiration to us all."
Dent's widow, Judy, told the local Northern Territory News newspaper that her husband of 20 years was still joking as he prepared to die in his Darwin home on Sunday.
"He was joking right to the end -- that's what Bob was like," she said. "He didn't want a big fuss made of him or for people to feel sorry for him."

The 66-year-old former carpenter was well known in this tropical frontier town in Australia's far north, said former territory leader Marshall Perron, the architect of the controversial euthanasia law.
"He was regarded as an excellent fellow. He was one of those blokes who goes through life not doing anyone any harm and making a contribution," Perron said.
Dent's son, Rod, hailed his father as a pioneer who fought for, and finally died for, his beliefs.
"My epitaph for my father is this: 'I loved you in life and I salute you in your death for your courage and your convictions. You died for the cause of euthanasia'."
A photo in the News shows a smiling, balding Dent dressed casually in shorts and an army-style shirt.
Friends described him as generous and caring.
"He helped a lot of cancer sufferers even when he was in pain himself -- he was the most genuine, kind and caring man I have met," said friend and fellow-Buddhist Alan Downes.
Dent first came to the vast, sparse outback territory in 1958 as a Church of England missionary, but left the church a few years later.
After he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, he turned to Buddhism. A dying man, he helped build a gold stupa, or traditional Buddhist spire, earlier this year.
"At that time, he was suffering quite extensively, but he would just not give up," Downes said.
